hooks.text: This smiling salamander can regrow its brain, yet it is nearly gone.
How can an animal that regrows its own brain face total extinction?
Only about 50 adult axolotls remain in their wild home.

title: The Smiling Salamander That Can Regrow Its Brain
description: Discover the incredible regenerative powers of the axolotl and the surprising crisis facing its last wild survivors in Mexico City.

beats.text: This smiling salamander can regrow its brain, yet it is nearly gone.
beats.visual: Leucistic axolotl color morph swimming in clear aquarium water, 2023

beats.text: Known as the axolotl, this aquatic amphibian keeps its external gills and never leaves the water.
beats.visual: External gills closeup of Ambystoma mexicanum wild type, Xochimilco

beats.text: Beyond staying young forever, it can completely regenerate severed limbs, tails, and heart tissue.
beats.visual: Scientific illustration of axolotl from Biodiversity Heritage Library, 1879

beats.text: Nearly all laboratory pets trace back to a single 1864 shipment sent to Paris.
beats.visual: Mexican 50 peso banknote featuring the axolotl, 2021

beats.text: Yet in the shrinking water channels of Lake [Xochimilco](/zˈOkˈImˈɪlkˈO/), the wild population has crashed.
beats.visual: Lake Xochimilco canals and trajineras in Mexico City, 2022

beats.text: Invasive fish like tilapia were introduced and eat their eggs, adding to pollution and urban pressure.
beats.visual: Tilapia swimming in freshwater wetland habitat

beats.text: Current surveys show that only about 50 to 1,000 adult axolotls survive in the wild.
beats.visual: Albino axolotl resting on a planted tank bottom

beats.text: This smiling salamander faces a fight to stay on Earth.
beats.visual: Wild type axolotl resting in natural habitat water

better_than_last: Integrated reviewer feedback by updating beat 6 to precisely explain how invasive tilapia were introduced and consume eggs alongside pollution and urban pressure.
